The convergence assumption has a desirable property: by 1990, the bulk of the adjustment (in terms of the composition of the absolute increase in the size of the labor force) will come from increased participation of young people facing the labor force entry decision for the first time. It seems highly likely that if opportunities exist, these young people will participate in a way increasingly similar to their age-sex counter-parts elsewhere in the U.S.
As mentioned previously, the economic assumptions allowed two different levels of peripheral Crow coal development activity. These alternative futures represent two baseline conditions, and include a projected low development level (AF-1) and a projected moderate level of development (AF-2).
Low development (AF-1) is essentially a projection of the <u>status-quo</u> with no development in coal or manufacturing and dwindling employment in agriculture over that existent in 1970. Moderate development (AF-2) assumes the mining of 32 million tons of Crow coal per year in the area of the Shell lease, plus an additional 10 million tons per year in other areas, all for shipment. Moderate development also assumes reduced employment in agriculture, and a small increase in manufacturing employment. As will be shown subsequently, the impact of Westmoreland's activities would be quite different under the two production level projections.
